slides.title: A man hiccuped for 68 years
slides.body: Charles Osborne started in 1922 after lifting a hog. They stopped in 1990, a year before he died.
slides.image_prompt: Old wooden farm barn at dusk with a large pig in straw, vintage 1920s atmosphere, warm light

slides.title: What a hiccup is
slides.body: Your diaphragm spasms and pulls in air. Your vocal cords slam shut a split second later. That's the 'hic'.
slides.image_prompt: Anatomical model of human lungs and diaphragm muscle on a dark background, dramatic lighting, medical illustration style

slides.title: It starts in the womb
slides.body: Ultrasounds show babies hiccuping long before birth. Newborns hiccup far more often than adults do.
slides.image_prompt: Glowing abstract ultrasound-style image of a curled fetus silhouette in soft blue tones, no text

slides.title: Nobody knows why
slides.body: One theory: it's a leftover reflex from amphibian ancestors, who pumped water over gills with their airways shut.
slides.image_prompt: Close-up of a tadpole swimming in clear green pond water, sunlight rays, visible gills

cta: Follow for a weird fact every day
caption:
Charles Osborne got the hiccups in 1922 while lifting a hog and didn't stop until 1990. Guinness World Records counts it as the longest attack ever, an estimated 430 million hics.

Every hiccup is a diaphragm spasm followed by your vocal cords snapping shut. You even did it in the womb. Scientists still aren't sure why, and one theory traces it back to gill breathing. Hiccups lasting over 48 hours are worth a doctor's visit. Sources: Guinness World Records, Mayo Clinic, Straus et al. (BioEssays, 2003).

What's your go-to hiccup cure, and does it actually work?
